newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore sees court as way out in island disputes.
newsitem.headline: Singapore sees court as way out in island disputes.

text.p: The Philippines should consider seeking arbitration by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in its island disputes with China, Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong told visiting Filipino journalists in an interview.
"Refer this matter if necessary to some international court," Goh said in the May 30 interview, the transcript of which was released by the government on Saturday.

Asked if China would agree to arbitration by the ICJ, Goh said, "I would not know China's thinking at this stage, but if the Philippines put it to the Chinese, then the Philippines is on high ground."

Goh said other ASEAN members would support the idea of referring the case to the ICJ. ASEAN comprises Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Brunei. Burma, Cambodia and Laos are due to join in July.

The Philippines and China are locked in heated exchanges over two sets of tiny islands in the South China Sea. One is a rocky outcrop called the Scarborough Shoal and the other involves parts of the Spratly Islands, a potentially oil-rich cluster of islets, reefs and atolls.
Recounting Singapore's experience, Goh said, "Like in our own dispute with Malaysia, we agreed that the best way to resolve this is to refer the matter to the ICJ."
"And because we have done that, Indonesia has also agreed with Malaysia to refer their own dispute of two islands, Sipadan and Ligitan, to the International Court.

Goh said he did not think these flashpoints of rival island claims would lead to conflict. "I mean, they could be irritants, they could be problems, but my sense is all leaders over here want to keep these disputes under control and solve them in a more civilised manner."

Turning to Burma, expected to be admitted shortly to ASEAN despite concerns over its policies expressed by human rights groups, Goh said it was not ASEAN members' style to interfere in each other's domestic politics.
"We make it very clear that the internal politics is entirely the countries' own preserve."
